stances.claim: Federalism is the cornerstone of Duterte's 'Change is coming' battle cry -- he passionately believes only federalism can solve the 'Imperial Manila' lament of Southern brethren and the centuries-old armed conflict in Mindanao, though he has not given details of his federalist concept.

Sovereign power is currently centralized in Metro Manila -- Congress enacts laws to which LGU ordinances must conform; the Manila-based president enforces via DILG; LGC devolution attempts (peace/order, IRAs) fall short because the Constitution mandates one national police and DBM can withhold IRAs; the 'too-powerful central government lording it over local governance, often ignorantly and ineffectively' is structurally embedded.

Federalism is not new to PH -- Salvador Araneta proposed it as 'Bayanikasan Constitution' at the 1971 ConCon and Jose Abueva (1971 ConCon secretary) wrote several papers -- but the 1986 Constitutional Commission did not seriously install it despite Davao-consultation discussions; making the present moment more an institutional revival than a new departure.

Instituting federalism will be difficult because PH government has always been centralized/unitary since Spanish/American colonial periods -- Filipinos look up to a 'father figure, a strong executive who dispenses governmental powers and largesse'; Duterte's election was predicated on personal charisma, the very quality he ironically needs to diffuse and devolve authority, and his promise to eradicate crime/drugs/corruption in 3-6 months 'can hardly happen if he does not have that central authority.'
stances.rhetorical_move: paradox-of-charisma framing (charisma as both election engine and devolution obstacle)

stances.claim: The party-list system serves as cautionary tale -- 'crafted rather hastily and haphazardly as an experiment in the Constitution and in the implementing law, uprooting from the European parliamentary system and planting it in our presidential form' -- now 'difficult to straighten out the confusion it has wrought'; making hasty federalist transplantation similarly inadvisable.
stances.rhetorical_move: cautionary-precedent argument (party-list as warning against hasty transplant)

stances.claim: Forms of government are 'born out of the experience and history of peoples and nations... not imported from foreign soils and implanted automatically' -- US federalism grew from the 13 colonies and Civil War; Malaysian federation from sultanates' common anti-British desire; PH federalism aspiration 'should be carved from our unique history as a nation' -- examining whether Mindanao-sultanate independent-historical streaks have parallels in Visayas and Luzon.
stances.rhetorical_move: evolutionary-not-imported framing with comparative historical-roots analysis

stances.claim: Duterte deserves leeway to implement his dreams for a better Philippines, but 'sufficient study, discussion and time are needed to craft a federal system suited to our needs, aspiration and history as a people' -- neither the 2-3 year timetable some proponents want nor a hasty constitutional transplant is responsible policy.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens his federalism series with 'Change is coming!' -- President-elect Rodrigo Duterte's battle cry -- whose cornerstone is his proposed shift to the federal system. Duterte passionately believes only federalism can solve the 'Imperial Manila' lament of Southern brethren and the centuries-old armed conflict in Mindanao, though he has not given details. Basically, federalism is the decentralization of sovereign powers to make government truly 'of the people, by the people and for the people' -- but sovereign power is currently centralized in Metro Manila, with the bicameral Congress enacting laws to which LGU ordinances must conform; theoretically the House of Representatives addresses local plight, but the economy's bounties take time, if ever, to trickle to the countryside. Law enforcement is centralized via the Manila-based president and DILG, leaving 'Imperial Manila' too far removed from the daily needs of the rural folks who constitute the vast majority. The Local Government Code attempted devolution (peace/order, Internal Revenue Allotments) but falls short because the Constitution mandates one national police (to which local police are legally beholden) and the DBM can withhold IRAs. Federalists want the Constitution to separate federal from local powers -- like the US system where the 50 states are constitutionally guaranteed exclusive powers the federal government cannot intrude into, and where much of US Supreme Court lawsuits address federal-state delineation. Federalism is not new to PH: Salvador Araneta proposed it as the 'Bayanikasan Constitution' at the 1971 ConCon, and Jose Abueva (1971 ConCon secretary) has written several papers on his version, though the 1986 Constitutional Commission did not seriously install federalism in the 1987 Constitution despite Davao-consultation discussions. Instituting federalism will be difficult because PH government has been centralized/unitary since Spanish and American colonial periods, with Filipinos looking up to 'a father figure, a strong executive who dispenses governmental powers and largesse.' Duterte's election was predicated largely on personal charisma -- 'the very quality he may need, ironically, to diffuse and devolve authority' -- and his promise to eradicate crime, drugs, and corruption in three to six months 'can hardly happen if he does not have that central authority.' It may not be possible to institute federalism in a 2-3-year timetable; Araneta believed 10-20 years; Abueva proposed two stages within 10 years. The party-list system serves as cautionary tale: 'crafted rather hastily and haphazardly as an experiment, uprooting from the European parliamentary system and planting it in our presidential form,' it is now 'difficult to straighten out the confusion it has wrought.' The forms and structures of governments are 'born out of the experience and history of peoples and nations... not imported from foreign soils and implanted automatically' -- US federalism grew from the 13 colonies and the Civil War between Northern Union and Southern Confederation; the Federation of Malaysia was born from various sultanates' common desire to be independent from British rule. PH federal aspiration 'should be carved from our unique history as a nation' -- examining whether the Mindanao sultanates' independent-historical streaks have parallels in Visayas and Luzon. At bottom, while Duterte deserves leeway to implement his dreams, 'sufficient study, discussion and time are needed to craft a federal system suited to our needs, aspiration and history as a people.'
